Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- An Ohio man who was suspended as the drum major of a band for giving President Obama a nod during last week's inaugural parade is calling it quits. John Coleman quit his band after it suspended him for nodding to President Obama last week. John Coleman resigned from the Cleveland Firefighters Memorial Pipes & Drums a week after the parade in Washington. Publicity about his suspension had gotten to be too much, he told CNN affiliate WEWS. "It's come to a point where I don't want embarrassment anymore between the pipe band and myself," Coleman, who is a firefighter, told WEWS on Tuesday. Coleman was seen during the nationally televised January 20 parade nodding toward the new president while marching with the band. A few steps later, he appeared to wave briefly. He told WEWS that as the band was marching past the grandstand where Obama was sitting, he made eye contact with the president. "Contact was made with our eyes both together and he smiled and waved at the band," he told the station. "And just as a gesture, I nodded my head. I gave him a slight wave and went on."  Watch parade and explanation » . Representatives from the group did not return calls from CNN. But bandleader Mike Engle told the Cleveland Plain Dealer that Coleman was suspended because he ignored military protocol. "We had gone over and over time and again with everyone in the band that this was a military parade," Engle told the newspaper. "Protocol and proper decorum had to be followed at all times. Unfortunately, John chose to ignore that." Coleman had been suspended from the band for six months. In a written statement, band manager Ken Rybka said Coleman's resignation from the group "comes as a shock and surprise." The band has been inundated with phone calls, e-mails and messages on its Internet pages -- almost all of them critical -- since the story first broke on Monday, Rybka said. iReport.com: 'Pretty cool thing that he acknowledged the president' "It is unfortunate that an internal band issue has raised so much discussion and ire from the general public," Rybka said in the statement. "It has disheartened me more than you can imagine." Rybka said that he will be taking a leave of absence from the band because of the furor. "The 'afterglow' of participating in the inaugural parade is gone," he said.

**(CNN) —** An Ohio man who was suspended from his role as a band’s drum major after nodding to President Obama during last week’s inaugural parade has decided to step down.

John Coleman resigned from the Cleveland Firefighters Memorial Pipes & Drums one week after the parade in Washington. He told CNN affiliate WEWS that the publicity surrounding his suspension had become too much.

“It’s come to a point where I don’t want embarrassment anymore between the pipe band and myself,” Coleman, a firefighter, told WEWS on Tuesday.

During the nationally televised January 20 parade, Coleman was seen nodding toward the newly inaugurated president while marching with the band. A few steps later, he appeared to wave briefly.

Coleman told WEWS that, as the band marched past the grandstand where Obama was seated, he made eye contact with the president.

“Contact was made with our eyes both together and he smiled and waved at the band,” Coleman told the station. “And just as a gesture, I nodded my head. I gave him a slight wave and went on.”

*Watch the parade and explanation »*

Representatives of the group did not return CNN’s calls. However, bandleader Mike Engle told the *Cleveland Plain Dealer* that Coleman was suspended for disregarding military protocol.

“We had gone over and over time and again with everyone in the band that this was a military parade,” Engle told the newspaper. “Protocol and proper decorum had to be followed at all times. Unfortunately, John chose to ignore that.”

Coleman had been suspended from the band for six months.

In a written statement, band manager Ken Rybka said Coleman’s resignation from the group “comes as a shock and surprise.”

Since the story first broke on Monday, the band has been inundated with phone calls, emails, and messages on its internet pages, nearly all of them critical, Rybka said.

*iReport.com: “Pretty cool thing that he acknowledged the president”*

“It is unfortunate that an internal band issue has raised so much discussion and ire from the general public,” Rybka said in the statement. “It has disheartened me more than you can imagine.”

Rybka said he would take a leave of absence from the band because of the furor.

“The ‘afterglow’ of participating in the inaugural parade is gone,” he said.

(CNN) — An Ohio firefighter has left the Cleveland Firefighters Memorial Pipes & Drums after the group suspended him from his role as drum major for acknowledging President Barack Obama during the previous week’s inaugural parade.

John Coleman submitted his resignation one week after the Washington parade. He told CNN affiliate WEWS that the attention surrounding his six-month suspension had become overwhelming. Speaking to the station Tuesday, Coleman said he wanted to prevent any further embarrassment for either himself or the band.

During the nationally broadcast parade on January 20, cameras captured Coleman dipping his head toward the newly inaugurated president and, moments later, apparently giving a short wave.

Coleman explained to WEWS that he and Obama made eye contact as the band passed the grandstand where the president was seated. According to Coleman, Obama smiled and waved at the musicians, prompting Coleman to respond with a small nod and brief wave before continuing along the parade route.

CNN’s calls to representatives of the organization were not returned. However, bandleader Mike Engle told the Cleveland Plain Dealer that Coleman had been disciplined for failing to observe military procedure. Engle said members had repeatedly been reminded that the event was a military parade and that appropriate conduct and protocol were required throughout, but Coleman did not comply.

Band manager Ken Rybka said in a written statement that Coleman’s decision to resign was unexpected. Since the story became public Monday, the group had received a flood of telephone calls, emails and posts on its online pages, nearly all expressing criticism, Rybka said.

An iReport.com comment described Coleman’s acknowledgment of the president as “a pretty cool thing.”

Rybka said he regretted that a matter originating within the band had generated so much public anger and debate, adding that the reaction had left him deeply discouraged. He also announced that he would temporarily step away from the group because of the controversy. In his words, any lingering sense of pride and excitement from taking part in the inaugural parade had disappeared.

John Coleman said he stepped down from the Cleveland Firefighters Memorial Pipes & Drums after the group imposed a six-month suspension over the gesture. Band leaders said members were expected to maintain military-style discipline and remain expressionless while marching.

### The incident

During Donald Trump’s inauguration on January 20, 2017, **Master Gunnery Sgt. Duane F. King**, then drum major of the U.S. Marine Band, was filmed giving outgoing President Barack Obama a brief nod as he passed. The subtle gesture circulated widely online and was interpreted by many as a personal sign of respect or farewell.

### Why it became controversial

Some social-media posts and commentators claimed King had violated military ceremonial protocol, arguing that a drum major should maintain strict bearing, face forward, and avoid unscripted political or personal gestures. More dramatic accounts suggested that he risked discipline or removal.

Others celebrated the nod as a dignified acknowledgment of the outgoing commander in chief, rather than a partisan statement.

### What the evidence showed

There was **no credible evidence that King was punished, relieved, or formally reprimanded**. Claims that the gesture constituted a serious protocol violation were largely unsupported and exaggerated online. Military drum majors routinely use head movements, eye contact, and other signals while directing formations, and acknowledging a president in a ceremonial setting is not inherently improper.

The episode therefore became less a genuine military scandal than a social-media controversy in which a momentary gesture was assigned competing political meanings. King continued serving as the Marine Band’s drum major after the inauguration.
